title: Research Explained #23 — Why We Paused the Physics to Build the Tools
html:
How a particle-accelerator idea, a software engineer's curiosity, and the need for trustworthy scientific computation led to BTLB-SIM.

A Question Worth Asking

When we began Beyond the Light Barrier, our primary interests were advanced communication, spacetime physics, and the possibility of discovering something useful about the limits of travel and communication.

We were not setting out to build a software development project.

And yet, much of our recent work has involved software architecture, validation, reproducibility, and questions about how scientific computations should be organized.

That raises a reasonable question:

Why did we pause some of the physics investigations to spend so much time building the tools?

The answer begins with a particle accelerator, an idea that emerged during a conversation on September 17, 2026, and a growing recognition that trustworthy scientific research requires more than equations and programs that produce numbers.

The Physics Question That Started It

In September 2026, our wormhole communication research was examining a possible precursor experiment involving the gravitational effects of a relativistic particle beam.

The idea was not to create a wormhole or demonstrate faster-than-light communication.

It was to investigate an effect predicted by accepted general relativity: the extremely small gravitational influence of energy and momentum carried by a high-energy particle beam.

Could an experimental arrangement distinguish such a signal from ordinary electromagnetic, mechanical, and other backgrounds associated with an accelerator?

Before answering that question, we needed to understand what the equations predicted, what an actual apparatus might measure, and whether the expected effect would be detectable.

That led us toward looking at existing particle accelerator facilities.

On September 17, we discussed several facilities, including CERN's Super Proton Synchrotron (SPS), its High Radiation to Materials facility (HiRadMat), and the Large Hadron Collider (LHC).

HiRadMat was particularly interesting as a possible setting for studying timing, instrumentation, and conventional backgrounds associated with an accelerator beam. The LHC provided a reference for a potentially more demanding future measurement.

We were not preparing a formal experiment proposal or seeking accelerator access.

I was simply curious about what facilities existed, what they could do, and when they operated.

During that investigation, we encountered information about CERN's operating schedules and Long Shutdown 3.

One of the documents discussed contained HiRadMat's 2026 operating schedule. Other historical CERN documentation confirms that beam operations were scheduled to end on August 31, 2026, with operations planned to resume in 2029.

That caught my attention.

Even if we eventually developed a scientifically worthwhile experiment, accelerator access would involve schedules, operational constraints, and circumstances beyond our immediate control.

And we had not yet established that our proposed measurement was feasible.

Looking into those practical limitations helped get me thinking about another possibility.

What if we could explore some of the same questions without needing access to a physical accelerator?

September 17: An Idea That Changed Our Direction

Later that evening, I interrupted our physics discussion with a side thought.

I said:

"I really wish that there was a simulated accelerator."

I wanted something that could help us understand what a physical experiment might be like.

I also made an important distinction: such an investigation would be a computational precursor, not a physical experiment.

That distinction was present from the beginning.

Within minutes, the idea acquired a name:

VAPE — Virtual Accelerator Precursor Experiment.

The initial scientific objective was relatively focused.

We wanted to explore whether simulated accelerator instrumentation could recover the gravitational signature predicted by accepted general relativity for a relativistic proton beam, while distinguishing that signature from conventional backgrounds.

A computational model could represent the particle source, calculate the predicted gravitational response under stated assumptions, model detector behavior, and investigate whether a proposed analysis could recover the expected signal.

That would not establish that an actual detector could observe the effect.

It would help us understand the mathematical and engineering requirements before attempting a physical experiment.

The possibility was exciting because it offered a way to investigate the problem while real-world experimental opportunities remained uncertain.

And within minutes of naming VAPE, I was already thinking about how to make the software modular.

The Plug-and-Play Idea Was There From the Beginning

Later that same evening, in a separate conversation, I began describing how I wanted the simulator to work.

Rather than building one large program designed around a single experiment, I wanted components that could be selected and connected according to the scientific question.

I described it as a module-based simulator in which we could activate particular modules when they were needed.

Then I extended that idea to sensors.

Different experiments might need different measurements. Why should every experiment carry the same instrumentation?

From my programming background, the natural answer was to define interfaces that would allow components to work together.

That meant application programming interfaces, or APIs.

A source model, a detector model, a sensor, and an analysis component should not have to be permanently welded together.

They should be capable of being assembled into an experiment appropriate to the question being investigated.

This was an architectural objective, not proof that we had already implemented or verified all those boundaries.

But the direction was clear: build reusable scientific capabilities rather than a one-purpose simulation.

There Was Also a Personal Motivation

I have spent much of my professional life developing software.

My career involved programming, software architecture, infrastructure systems, and the engineering challenges that arise when complex systems have to work reliably.

After retiring, I remained interested in learning new technologies and exploring what modern programming tools could make possible.

Python was one of the languages I wanted to learn more deeply. Rust was another.

Both were relevant to the kind of computational work we were considering, although in different ways.

Python offered an accessible environment for scientific programming, numerical libraries, experimentation, and orchestration.

Rust offered opportunities to investigate compiled performance, memory safety, and carefully defined interfaces between components.

That did not mean every scientific calculation needed to be written in Rust, or that a compiled language would automatically be faster than an optimized numerical library.

It meant we had an opportunity to learn which tools were appropriate for which responsibilities.

VAPE therefore became more than an interesting physics idea.

It was also an opportunity to combine scientific curiosity with decades of software-engineering experience while learning new approaches to computational research.

Learning a Different Kind of Software Engineering

One of the interesting things about this work is that scientific software presents some challenges that are different from those encountered in ordinary application development.

That does not mean conventional software engineering lacks rigor.

Safety-critical systems, financial infrastructure, operating systems, and other demanding applications can require extensive verification, traceability, reproducibility, and formal controls.

But scientific software has an additional responsibility: it must preserve the relationship between a computation and the scientific claim someone might make from its result.

A program can execute successfully and still produce a scientifically misleading answer.

Perhaps the equation was implemented incorrectly.

Perhaps the numerical method was unsuitable for the problem.

Perhaps the calculation lacked sufficient precision.

Perhaps the boundary conditions were wrong.

Or perhaps the computation was correct, but the underlying physical model was incomplete or inapplicable.

Those are different failure modes, and they should not be treated as interchangeable.

Likewise, a numerical result that agrees with a published calculation does not automatically establish independent scientific reproduction.

If both implementations depend on the same mistaken assumption, agreement may simply reproduce the mistake.

This is why we began paying closer attention to the distinction between software correctness, numerical verification, model validation, independent reproduction, and physical experiment.

They are related, but they are not the same thing.

From VAPE to BTLB-SIM

As we worked through the initial VAPE design, another question emerged.

Why should the reusable parts of the simulator belong exclusively to VAPE?

Our broader Beyond the Light Barrier research includes wormhole communication, advanced propulsion, and other investigations involving mathematical models, numerical calculations, and potentially testable predictions.

Those investigations could benefit from some of the same supporting capabilities.

Experiment configuration.

Execution coordination.

Validation and numerical diagnostics.

Artifact preservation.

Provenance and reproducibility records.

Interfaces between scientific components.

Instead of placing all those responsibilities inside a virtual accelerator application, we began separating the general scientific infrastructure from the physics of any particular experiment.

That broader framework became BTLB-SIM.

VAPE could then be treated as an application using the framework rather than as the framework itself.

This distinction remains an architectural objective subject to verification. It does not mean every intended interface or responsibility boundary has already been successfully established.

Why Simulation Could Be Valuable

Simulation can help us investigate questions that would be difficult, expensive, or premature to approach with physical hardware.

For example, before building a detector, we might want to know whether the predicted signal has a distinctive mathematical signature.

We might want to investigate how that signature changes when source geometry, timing, or detector placement changes.

We might want to compare alternative numerical methods or determine whether a proposed measurement is dominated by an expected background.

We can also test software and analysis procedures using synthetic signals whose properties are known in advance.

That can reveal mistakes in an analysis pipeline before anyone attempts to interpret real measurements.

These are legitimate uses of computational experiments.

But their conclusions remain limited by the equations, assumptions, input data, numerical methods, and simulated conditions.

A simulation can help determine what a proposed experiment should look for.

It cannot establish that nature will produce the predicted result.

A Simulation Is Not a Physical Experiment

This distinction is central to the Beyond the Light Barrier Research Method.

When we simulate a relativistic particle beam, we are not creating an actual particle beam.

When we calculate a gravitational response, we are not measuring a gravitational field in a laboratory.

When a simulated detector recovers an injected signal, we have not demonstrated that a physical detector could recover that signal under real operating conditions.

What we have demonstrated, within the limits of the computational test, is that a specified model and analysis procedure behaved in a particular way.

That can be useful evidence about the software, mathematics, or proposed experimental design.

It is not evidence that a wormhole exists, that faster-than-light communication is possible, or that an advanced propulsion mechanism has been physically demonstrated.

Keeping those distinctions visible protects the value of the work.

Why Not Just Write the Software?

Given my background, it might seem reasonable to simply write the program, test it, and move on.

For a small, narrowly defined calculation, that may be exactly the right approach.

Not every scientific question requires a large framework.

But once we began considering reusable scientific infrastructure, the problem changed.

We needed to ask what information an experiment must preserve so that someone can later determine exactly what was calculated.

Which model was used?

Which version of the equations?

Which assumptions and boundary conditions?

Which software implementation?

Which parameters and numerical methods?

What did the verification checks actually establish?

And what remained uncertain?

These questions affect the architecture because information that is never captured during execution may be impossible to reconstruct reliably afterward.

We also discovered that some seemingly simple software behaviors become much harder to reason about when concurrency, interruption, recovery, module boundaries, and historical records are involved.

That is where the architecture itself began to require serious investigation.

When the Architecture Became the Research

BTLB-SIM eventually reached a point where we needed to examine whether its own execution and record-keeping architecture could satisfy the obligations we were placing upon it.

That led to the AR-1.7 Architecture Stress Audit.

The purpose of the audit was not to prove that the architecture was correct.

It was to challenge the architecture and preserve what the investigation revealed.

Some results exposed unresolved questions about execution ordering, source semantics, ownership, provenance, and the relationships between source-level operations and project-level records.

These were software and architecture findings, not experimental discoveries about spacetime.

The investigation eventually reached a formally bounded closure.

That closure was a successful completion of the defined investigative work, not acceptance of the architecture.

Eight findings remained open.

The closure record explicitly preserved the distinction between completing an investigation and resolving the problems discovered by that investigation.

Another investigation, CP107-R1, received a REVISE classification because the required source-to-project target correspondence had not been established sufficiently.

That was not proof that the entire architecture was impossible or invalid.

It meant a specific proposed semantic justification remained incomplete.

Rather than quietly assuming the missing relationship existed, we preserved the limitation.

This may sound like an unusual amount of attention to software details for a project concerned with advanced physics.

But if a research framework cannot reliably explain what it executed, how it interpreted an operation, or how it preserved a result, then its scientific conclusions may become difficult to audit.

Questioning the Architecture Itself

At that point, another important question emerged.

Were we trying too hard to preserve an architecture simply because we had already invested time in it?

That would be a mistake.

The same scientific discipline that requires us to challenge a physical hypothesis should also apply to our software design assumptions.

We should not protect a particular architecture from contrary evidence.

Nor should we assume that discovering a problem means the entire design must be discarded.

The appropriate response is to determine what the evidence actually supports.

That led to the Next Architecture Exploration effort, or NAE-1.

Its adopted charter deliberately leaves multiple possibilities open.

We might evolve the existing architecture.

We might refine its module boundaries.

We might adopt a hybrid approach.

We might discover that different scientific applications require different execution architectures.

Or we might conclude that a clean-sheet design is justified.

No particular outcome is assumed in advance.

And adopting the exploration charter does not itself authorize implementation or establish that a future architecture has been accepted.

Have We Made This Too Complicated?

That is a question worth asking, especially when a project that began with advanced physics finds itself investigating software architecture in considerable detail.

Complexity is not automatically evidence of sophistication.

Sometimes it is evidence that we have introduced unnecessary machinery.

A good scientific tool should be no more complicated than necessary to meet its actual requirements.

But simplicity cannot mean ignoring obligations that matter.

If we simplify a system by discarding the information needed to reproduce or interpret a result, we may have made the software easier to write while making the science less trustworthy.

The challenge is to find the appropriate balance.

We should be willing to simplify, replace, or retire architectural ideas that do not justify their cost.

And we should be equally willing to preserve mechanisms that are necessary to maintain scientific integrity.

Does the Physics Have to Wait?

Not necessarily.

The existence of unresolved BTLB-SIM architecture questions does not mean every physics investigation must stop.

Some questions can be addressed analytically.

Others can be investigated with small, independently specified numerical programs.

Published results can be checked against alternative derivations or implementations.

And some exploratory questions may not require BTLB-SIM at all.

The important requirement is that the method used should be appropriate to the scientific claim being made.

Where a framework is not yet sufficiently verified, we should not represent its output as more authoritative than the evidence permits.

Where a simpler method is adequate, we should use it.

Where a complex, reusable system genuinely provides value, we should develop and verify it with care.

Our goal is not to make every future physics investigation dependent on completing one enormous software project.

It is to build the capabilities that genuinely improve the reliability and usefulness of our research.

What Would Make the Investment Worthwhile?

The value of BTLB-SIM should ultimately be judged by what it enables us to investigate and how reliably those investigations can be reproduced and evaluated.

Can it help us identify mistakes earlier?

Can it preserve the assumptions and numerical details needed to understand a result?

Can it support independent checks rather than merely repeating its own conclusions?

Can it make it easier to compare models without confusing their assumptions?

Can it help us determine when a proposed experiment is not feasible, before significant resources are committed?

Can it preserve negative results so that future work does not unknowingly repeat failed approaches?

And can it do these things without becoming so complicated that maintaining the framework consumes the research program?

Those are the questions that should determine whether the investment is worthwhile.

Closing Reflection

When I suggested a simulated accelerator on September 17, I was thinking about a practical problem.

We were studying a physical effect that might someday be worth measuring, but we did not have a particle accelerator or a demonstrated measurement architecture.

I wondered whether software could help us explore the problem first.

Within minutes, that thought became VAPE.

Then my software-engineering instincts took over. I wanted modules, selectable sensors, and APIs that would let us assemble experiments without rebuilding everything from scratch.

From there, the work grew into BTLB-SIM and eventually into a much broader examination of what trustworthy scientific computation requires.

We did not begin with the intention of spending so much time on software architecture.

But the questions we encountered were real, and ignoring them would not have made them disappear.

We have also learned that building tools can become its own distraction if we lose sight of why we wanted them.

That is why the architecture must remain open to criticism, simplification, and even replacement.

The tools exist to serve the research. The research does not exist to justify the tools.

We still want to understand what physics permits.

We still want to investigate advanced communication, spacetime, and propulsion without assuming that any particular speculative mechanism must succeed.

And we still want to find experiments that could genuinely test the ideas worth pursuing.

For now, part of that journey involves making sure that when our software tells us something interesting, we can explain exactly what it means, what supports it, and what remains unknown.

That is why we paused some of the physics to build the tools.

    physically demonstrated.
  

  
Keeping those distinctions visible protects the value of the work.

  
Why Not Just Write the Software?

  

    Given my background, it might seem reasonable to simply write the program,
    test it, and move on.
  

  

    For a small, narrowly defined calculation, that may be exactly the right
    approach.
  

  
Not every scientific question requires a large framework.

  

    But once we began considering reusable scientific infrastructure, the
    problem changed.
  

  

    We needed to ask what information an experiment must preserve so that
    someone can later determine exactly what was calculated.
  

  
Which model was used?

  
Which version of the equations?

  
Which assumptions and boundary conditions?

  
Which software implementation?

  
Which parameters and numerical methods?

  
What did the verification checks actually establish?

  
And what remained uncertain?

  

    These questions affect the architecture because information that is never
    captured during execution may be impossible to reconstruct reliably
    afterward.
  

  

    We also discovered that some seemingly simple software behaviors become much
    harder to reason about when concurrency, interruption, recovery, module
    boundaries, and historical records are involved.
  

  

    That is where the architecture itself began to require serious
    investigation.
  

  
When the Architecture Became the Research

  

    BTLB-SIM eventually reached a point where we needed to examine whether its
    own execution and record-keeping architecture could satisfy the obligations
    we were placing upon it.
  

  
That led to the AR-1.7 Architecture Stress Audit.

  

    The purpose of the audit was not to prove that the architecture was correct.
  

  

    It was to challenge the architecture and preserve what the investigation
    revealed.
  

  

    Some results exposed unresolved questions about execution ordering, source
    semantics, ownership, provenance, and the relationships between source-level
    operations and project-level records.
  

  

    These were software and architecture findings, not experimental discoveries
    about spacetime.
  

  
The investigation eventually reached a formally bounded closure.

  

    That closure was a successful completion of the defined investigative work,
    not acceptance of the architecture.
  

  
Eight findings remained open.

  

    The closure record explicitly preserved the distinction between completing
    an investigation and resolving the problems discovered by that
    investigation.
  

  

    Another investigation, CP107-R1, received a REVISE classification because
    the required source-to-project target correspondence had not been
    established sufficiently.
  

  

    That was not proof that the entire architecture was impossible or invalid.
  

  

    It meant a specific proposed semantic justification remained incomplete.
  

  

    Rather than quietly assuming the missing relationship existed, we preserved
    the limitation.
  

  

    This may sound like an unusual amount of attention to software details for a
    project concerned with advanced physics.
  

  

    But if a research framework cannot reliably explain what it executed, how it
    interpreted an operation, or how it preserved a result, then its scientific
    conclusions may become difficult to audit.
  

  
Questioning the Architecture Itself

  
At that point, another important question emerged.

  

    Were we trying too hard to preserve an architecture simply because we had
    already invested time in it?
  

  
That would be a mistake.

  

    The same scientific discipline that requires us to challenge a physical
    hypothesis should also apply to our software design assumptions.
  

  
We should not protect a particular architecture from contrary evidence.

  

    Nor should we assume that discovering a problem means the entire design must
    be discarded.
  

  

    The appropriate response is to determine what the evidence actually
    supports.
  

  
That led to the Next Architecture Exploration effort, or NAE-1.

  
Its adopted charter deliberately leaves multiple possibilities open.

  
We might evolve the existing architecture.

  
We might refine its module boundaries.

  
We might adopt a hybrid approach.

  

    We might discover that different scientific applications require different
    execution architectures.
  

  
Or we might conclude that a clean-sheet design is justified.

  
No particular outcome is assumed in advance.

  

    And adopting the exploration charter does not itself authorize
    implementation or establish that a future architecture has been accepted.
  

  
Have We Made This Too Complicated?

  

    That is a question worth asking, especially when a project that began with
    advanced physics finds itself investigating software architecture in
    considerable detail.
  

  
Complexity is not automatically evidence of sophistication.

  
Sometimes it is evidence that we have introduced unnecessary machinery.

  

    A good scientific tool should be no more complicated than necessary to meet
    its actual requirements.
  

  
But simplicity cannot mean ignoring obligations that matter.

  

    If we simplify a system by discarding the information needed to reproduce or
    interpret a result, we may have made the software easier to write while
    making the science less trustworthy.
  

  
The challenge is to find the appropriate balance.

  

    We should be willing to simplify, replace, or retire architectural ideas
    that do not justify their cost.
  

  

    And we should be equally willing to preserve mechanisms that are necessary
    to maintain scientific integrity.
  

  
Does the Physics Have to Wait?

  
Not necessarily.

  

    The existence of unresolved BTLB-SIM architecture questions does not mean
    every physics investigation must stop.
  

  
Some questions can be addressed analytically.

  

    Others can be investigated with small, independently specified numerical
    programs.
  

  

    Published results can be checked against alternative derivations or
    implementations.
  

  
And some exploratory questions may not require BTLB-SIM at all.

  

    The important requirement is that the method used should be appropriate to
    the scientific claim being made.
  

  

    Where a framework is not yet sufficiently verified, we should not represent
    its output as more authoritative than the evidence permits.
  

  
Where a simpler method is adequate, we should use it.

  

    Where a complex, reusable system genuinely provides value, we should develop
    and verify it with care.
  

  

    Our goal is not to make every future physics investigation dependent on
    completing one enormous software project.
  

  

    It is to build the capabilities that genuinely improve the reliability and
    usefulness of our research.
  

  
What Would Make the Investment Worthwhile?

  

    The value of BTLB-SIM should ultimately be judged by what it enables us to
    investigate and how reliably those investigations can be reproduced and
    evaluated.
  

  
Can it help us identify mistakes earlier?

  

    Can it preserve the assumptions and numerical details needed to understand a
    result?
  

  

    Can it support independent checks rather than merely repeating its own
    conclusions?
  

  

    Can it make it easier to compare models without confusing their assumptions?
  

  

    Can it help us determine when a proposed experiment is not feasible, before
    significant resources are committed?
  

  

    Can it preserve negative results so that future work does not unknowingly
    repeat failed approaches?
  

  

    And can it do these things without becoming so complicated that maintaining
    the framework consumes the research program?
  

  

    Those are the questions that should determine whether the investment is
    worthwhile.
  

  
Closing Reflection

  

    When I suggested a simulated accelerator on September 17, I was thinking
    about a practical problem.
  

  

    We were studying a physical effect that might someday be worth measuring,
    but we did not have a particle accelerator or a demonstrated measurement
    architecture.
  

  
I wondered whether software could help us explore the problem first.

  
Within minutes, that thought became VAPE.

  

    Then my software-engineering instincts took over. I wanted modules,
    selectable sensors, and APIs that would let us assemble experiments without
    rebuilding everything from scratch.
  

  

    From there, the work grew into BTLB-SIM and eventually into a much broader
    examination of what trustworthy scientific computation requires.
  

  

    We did not begin with the intention of spending so much time on software
    architecture.
  

  

    But the questions we encountered were real, and ignoring them would not have
    made them disappear.
  

  

    We have also learned that building tools can become its own distraction if
    we lose sight of why we wanted them.
  

  

    That is why the architecture must remain open to criticism, simplification,
    and even replacement.
  

  

    The tools exist to serve the research. The research does not exist to
      justify the tools.
  

  
We still want to understand what physics permits.

  

    We still want to investigate advanced communication, spacetime, and
    propulsion without assuming that any particular speculative mechanism must
    succeed.
  

  

    And we still want to find experiments that could genuinely test the ideas
    worth pursuing.
  

  

    For now, part of that journey involves making sure that when our software
    tells us something interesting, we can explain exactly what it means, what
    supports it, and what remains unknown.
  

  
That is why we paused some of the physics to build the tools.
